row_description: A child learns to swap a yell for an indoor voice when reminded, and to scream only for fun or danger. Clear rules, praise for trying and a shared signal help self-control grow gradually.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative with a complication or constraint added (time pressure, little money, a noisy place, a missing person, bad weather), still faithful to the row.

record.passage: The heavy traffic outside the Toronto clinic drowned out every sound, and Thomas, five, screamed "Chinmay, look, a helicopter!" at his uncle, standing right beside him. Chinmay smiled and touched his ear. "Here, outdoors, that voice is fine. Inside the clinic, use the quiet one." Inside, Thomas remembered, pointed at the card that his uncle had shown him, and whispered, "Shh voice." "Well done," whispered Chinmay. When the nurse called them, Thomas held the card up to show her.

qa.q: What did Thomas see outside the clinic?
qa.a: He saw a helicopter.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when he screamed about the helicopter?
qa.a: He was excited and wanted to share it. The traffic was loud, so he may also have thought he needed to shout to be heard.

qa.q: What could Chinmay do to help Thomas use the right voice in future?
qa.a: He can keep using the card and a friendly reminder, and praise Thomas whenever he tries.

qa.q: How might the nurse see Thomas holding up the card?
qa.a: She might find it charming and understand that he is learning to control his voice.

record.grounding: A child learns to swap a yell for an indoor voice, and a shared signal and praise help.

row_description: A teenager writes in capitals, many exclamation marks or dramatic emojis, which may be play, real intensity or performing for followers. Tone online is easy to misread, so a quick check helps.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in an urban Indian setting (city flat, colony, market, school, office).

record.passage: Himani posted a story that evening: "I CANNOT BELIEVE THIS!!!!!! 😱 my life is a disaster." Under it was a photo of her test paper. Within minutes people were reacting with laughing faces and "same!!". Pallavi, sitting in her own room, wasn't sure what to think. Himani had a habit of dramatic posts for her followers, and she also had a real habit of caring too much about marks. Pallavi typed a private message instead of joining the reactions: "Hey, is that a joke-dramatic or a really-upset one? I'm around either way." Three dots appeared, vanished, appeared again. Then: "Honestly, a little of both. I'll call you in ten minutes." Pallavi put the phone down, relieved she'd asked.

qa.q: What did Himani's story show under the caption?
qa.a: It showed a photo of her test paper.

qa.q: What might Himani be feeling when she posts the story?
qa.a: Probably a mix of real upset about the marks and a wish to be seen and joined by her followers, and she admits it is a little of both.

qa.q: Why was a private message better than adding a reaction?
qa.a: The public reactions treated the post as a joke, while a private check gave Himani room to say if some of it was real.

qa.q: How might the followers have read the post differently from Pallavi?
qa.a: They only saw capitals and an emoji and took it as playful, while Pallavi knew Himani's habits and worried about the real feeling under it.

record.grounding: A teen's capitals and dramatic emoji may be play, real intensity or performing for followers, and a quick private check helps.

row_description: A young adult offers a hand on the shoulder or a hug to a grieving friend and watches for signs of acceptance. Touch can soothe but may not suit everyone; asking can I hug you respects choice and shows care.
recipe_text: First-person reflective account by the protagonist, looking back a little (for 7-12 keep it simple and short).

record.subtype: Comfort touch in grief and care [Interpreting]
record.passage: I did not know what to do when Hrithik's father died. We were in the courtyard after the ceremony and Hrithik stood alone, arms crossed, looking at the ground. I wanted to hug him but stopped myself. I am Tejas, and I have known him since school, but I also remember that my own cousin hated being held when she was grieving. So I stood close and said, "Can I hug you, or would you rather I just stay here?" Hrithik was quiet, then nodded and stepped forward. We stood for a while. Afterwards he said asking helped, because he could not have said it himself. I still do not know what was right for anyone else.

qa.q: Where was Hrithik standing after the ceremony?
qa.a: He stood alone in the courtyard.

qa.q: Why did Tejas hold back from hugging at once, and what was Tejas feeling?
qa.a: Tejas wanted to comfort Hrithik but remembered a cousin who hated being held while grieving. Tejas was unsure what suited the friend, so asked first.

qa.q: What made Tejas's approach caring?
qa.a: Tejas asked "Can I hug you" and offered to just stay, so Hrithik could choose either.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have felt when asked, given the crossed arms and silence?
qa.a: Hrithik may have felt too overwhelmed to say what was needed, so a simple question that gave choice was a relief.

record.grounding: Reflective account of a young adult offering a hug to a grieving friend by asking first and watching for acceptance.

row_description: A school-age child argues "Everyone else is allowed" or "I finished my homework, so..." to persuade. Reasons can be valid or exaggerated, and adults can respond to the argument while noting the limits.
recipe_text: Dialogue-heavy family or home scene (mostly spoken lines, little narration), any setting.

record.passage: “Everyone else in my class is allowed a phone,” said Gopika at dinner. Her father put down his spoon. “Everyone? Every single one?” Gopika hesitated. “Well, most.” “How many exactly?” “Three, I think.” Her father nodded. “Thank you for being honest. What is your reason?” “I finished my homework, so I should be able to chat with friends.” Arnab, her brother, said, “That's a real reason.” Her father said, “It's a fair argument, but a phone at your age isn't something we're ready for yet. What about using my phone for half an hour on weekends?” Gopika thought. “Okay.”

qa.q: How many classmates did Gopika say had phones once she was asked exactly?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: Why did Gopika say everyone else was allowed a phone, and what changed when her father asked?
qa.a: She wanted to persuade him, but when asked she admitted it was only about three, so exaggeration gave way to honesty.

qa.q: How did Gopika's father respond well?
qa.a: He thanked her for being honest, took her reason seriously, and offered a limited alternative while explaining his limit.

qa.q: How might Arnab have seen the argument?
qa.a: He thought the reason about finishing homework was fair, so he probably wanted to support his sister.

record.grounding: A child argues everyone else is allowed and I finished my homework so, and the adult responds to the argument while noting limits.

row_description: A teenager with heavy, half-closed eyes after late screen time may look bored or rude in class, but is often simply tired. Adults can ask about sleep before assuming disrespect.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in an urban Indian setting (city flat, colony, market, school, office).

record.passage: Mr Arnab, the maths teacher, had taught Gopika for two years, and she was usually first with her hand up. Today her eyelids were heavy and half closed, her head propped on her palm. When he asked a question she took a while to look up. A few classmates smirked. Arnab felt a flash of irritation and thought, is she being rude? He held it back. After the bell he said, "Gopika, you seem very tired today. How has your sleep been?" She rubbed her red eyes. "I was on my phone till two, sir, finishing a project video. Sorry." He nodded. "Thank you for telling me. Let us talk about how to space it out."

qa.q: What was Gopika's head propped on?
qa.a: Gopika's head was propped on her palm.

qa.q: What did Arnab think when he first saw Gopika's half-closed eyes?
qa.a: He felt irritation and wondered if she was being rude, but held it back. He then chose to ask about sleep, since tiredness was another likely reason.

qa.q: What did Arnab do that avoided assuming disrespect?
qa.a: He asked how her sleep had been, listened to her answer and offered to talk about spacing the work out.

qa.q: How might Gopika have felt when the classmates smirked?
qa.a: She was probably embarrassed and too tired to respond, and may have worried she looked disrespectful.

record.grounding: A teenager with half-closed eyes after late screen time may look rude but is simply tired, and an adult asks about sleep first.

row_description: A teenager may find it hard to apologise because it feels like losing status, so may joke, send a meme or act as if nothing happened. Repair is usually stronger with a short plain acknowledgement.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative with a complication or constraint added (time pressure, little money, a noisy place, a missing person, bad weather), still faithful to the row.

record.passage: The bus to the football ground was leaving in ten minutes and Yogesh's phone buzzed twice. Dhruv, angry, had written: 'You forgot the plan again.' Yogesh had promised to bring the ball and left it at home. His first thought was a meme of a sad cat with the caption 'my bad lol'. He typed it, hovered, and deleted it. On the noisy platform, with shouting all around, he typed instead, 'I forgot the ball. That was on me, I'm sorry. I'll run home and get it and meet you at the ground.' Dhruv answered after a minute: 'ok. thanks for saying it.' Yogesh let out a breath. It didn't feel small at all.

qa.q: What had Yogesh forgotten to bring?
qa.a: He forgot to bring the ball.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh delete the meme before sending it?
qa.a: He probably sensed the joke would sound like he was avoiding the mistake, and he wanted to own it. The pull toward a joke shows how uncomfortable apologising felt.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do next after his apology?
qa.a: He can follow through on what he offered, going home for the ball and meeting Dhruv at the ground.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt on reading the plain apology?
qa.a: He probably felt heard and less angry, which is why he wrote 'thanks for saying it'.

record.grounding: A teen avoids a face-saving joke and gives a short plain apology.

row_description: A child puts a hand over the mouth after a slip, in giggles or in shy surprise. It may signal embarrassment, mischief or awe; context tells which, and a gentle smile helps a child feel safe.
recipe_text: Scene set inside an institution: school, hostel, clinic waiting room, workplace, sports club, community centre.

record.subtype: Covering the mouth when shy or surprised [Expressing]
record.passage: Group time at a Lucknow school. Ira, the teacher, held up a picture of a giant tortoise, and Aadhya, five, gasped and covered her mouth with both hands, eyes shining. Then Ira asked the class who could name the animal. Aadhya's hand went to her mouth again, and she looked at the floor. "Tortoise," she whispered through her fingers. "Yes!" said Ira warmly, smiling. Aadhya lowered her hand a little, and gave a small smile back.

qa.q: What did Aadhya do when she saw the picture of the tortoise?
qa.a: She gasped and covered her mouth with both hands.

qa.q: What could Aadhya's hand over her mouth mean on the second occasion?
qa.a: It probably showed shyness about speaking up in front of everyone, and the first time it seemed to show awe. Her whisper and looking down support shyness.

qa.q: How does Ira's smile help Aadhya?
qa.a: It tells Aadhya her answer was welcome and that it is safe to speak, so she smiles back.

qa.q: How might the other children see Aadhya's hand over her mouth?
qa.a: They may think she is giggling or hiding something, and might not realise she is shy.

record.grounding: A child covers her mouth in awe and in shyness, and context and a gentle smile help.

row_description: A preschooler follows short one-step instructions and needs reminders that are calm and repeated. Long lists or a scolding tone reduce cooperation, so a child benefits from being shown as well.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in a rural or small-town Indian setting (village, farm, kasba, local bus, temple fair, small shop).

record.passage: On the farm in Punjab, Gurpreet had a list in her head: wash hands, bring the plates, set out the water. Her daughter Madhuri, five, got lost after "wash hands" and stood by the tap, dripping. Gurpreet breathed out, knelt and said calmly, "Just the plates now." Madhuri carried them over. "Now the water jug," said Gurpreet, walking beside her. Madhuri smiled. "One by one."

qa.q: What did Gurpreet ask Madhuri to carry after washing hands?
qa.a: The plates.

qa.q: How might Madhuri have felt standing by the tap, dripping?
qa.a: Lost or unsure what to do next, since the list was long. She might also just have been enjoying the water.

qa.q: What made Gurpreet's second try work better?
qa.a: She gave one short step at a time in a calm voice and walked beside her.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel when Madhuri says "One by one"?
qa.a: Probably relieved and pleased that the calmer way worked.

record.grounding: Shows a preschooler following one-step instructions and getting lost in a long list, helped by calm repeated reminders.

row_description: A young adult views a painting or film and forms a view of the maker's mood. Art reflects craft, tradition and audience as well as feeling, so the maker's state cannot be safely inferred from the work alone.
recipe_text: Dialogue-heavy family or home scene (mostly spoken lines, little narration), any setting.

record.passage:
"This film is so dark," Aditi said as the credits rolled in the dorm lounge. "The director must be depressed."
"Maybe," Zainab said, tucking her feet under her. "Or he might just love that style. Lots of films from his country are like that."
"But every scene is at night."
"That's a choice. It can be a craft thing or a story thing. It doesn't have to say how he feels in his own life."
Aditi frowned. "So I can't say anything?"
"You can say what it did to you. It made you feel low, right?"
"It did. I felt like I'd been left in a cold room."
"That's a good thing to know. Just don't diagnose the man."

qa.q: When are the scenes in the film set?
qa.a: Every scene is at night.

qa.q: What does Aditi feel about the film, and what did she wrongly assume about the director?
qa.a: Aditi felt low, like she'd been left in a cold room, and she assumed the director must be depressed.

qa.q: What could Aditi do to talk about the film without guessing the director's state?
qa.a: She could describe what it did to her and what choices she noticed, like the night scenes.

qa.q: How might the director see Aditi's guess about his mood?
qa.a: He might find it odd, since darkness in a film can come from style, tradition or story rather than his own feelings.

record.grounding: Aditi and Zainab discuss a film and learn that a maker's mood cannot be safely inferred from the work.

row_description: A toddler buries the face in a parent's shoulder or hides behind legs when meeting strangers. It signals shyness or fear rather than rudeness; letting the child warm up at their own pace supports trust.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative set outside India (any country), ordinary everyday detail.

record.passage: At the door of their house in Melbourne, a neighbour bent down and said, “And who's this?” Felix, two, pushed his face into his mother Mei's shoulder and gripped her shirt with both fists. “He's shy,” said Mei, keeping her hand on his back. The neighbour nodded and talked to Mei about the weather. Felix peeked out with one eye, then went behind her legs. When the neighbour left, he waved from behind Mei's knee, still half hidden.

qa.q: Where did Felix hide his face?
qa.a: In his mother Mei's shoulder.

qa.q: What might Felix's hiding and peeking show, and what else could it be?
qa.a: It probably shows shyness or fear of a stranger, and the peeking shows curiosity. It could also be tiredness, but his wave at the end shows he warmed up.

qa.q: What could Mei do to help him feel comfortable?
qa.a: She could let him stay close, talk to the neighbour herself and let Felix say hello when he is ready.

qa.q: How might the neighbour feel about Felix hiding?
qa.a: She may feel a little awkward, but seeing Mei calm helps her understand it is not rudeness.

record.grounding: A toddler buries his face in a parent's shoulder and hides behind her legs with a stranger, signalling shyness or fear.

row_description: A teenager invites friends or appeals to a parent for later curfew with reasons. Appeals with respectful tone and evidence more often succeed than pressure and threats.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in a rural or small-town Indian setting (village, farm, kasba, local bus, temple fair, small shop).

record.passage: Anand had worked out his speech while feeding the buffaloes. When his mother Disha came back from the well, he did not sulk about the mela as he had last year. "Ma, the evening aarti at the temple fair is at seven. Can I stay till the last bus at eight-thirty?" Disha kept wringing her dupatta. "Who else is going?" "Cousin Dev and two boys from school. I finished the fodder and I'll carry the phone. I'll call from the bus stand." She looked at him a long moment. "If you call, and you're back by nine, then yes. We'll see how it goes and talk again next time." Anand nodded, smiled, and did not push for more.

qa.q: Where was Anand when he prepared his request?
qa.a: He was feeding the buffaloes.

qa.q: What does Anand want from his mother, and what in his behaviour suggests it?
qa.a: He hopes to stay for the evening aarti at the mela and wants her trust, shown by his prepared speech and the reasons he gives. He is trying not to sulk as he did last year.

qa.q: What made Disha say yes?
qa.a: His respectful tone, the concrete details about who is going and when he will call, and the fact that he finished his chores made the request easier to trust.

qa.q: How might Disha feel as she agrees?
qa.a: She may feel a little worried, yet proud that he asked properly, so a trial for one evening feels reasonable. 🙂

record.grounding: A teen appeals to a parent with reasons and a respectful tone, and it works better than pressure.

row_description: A young adult at a wedding or a reunion cries and smiles at once, feeling joy, relief and loss together. Mixed displays are ordinary, and a listener can simply ask or share the moment.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in a rural or small-town Indian setting (village, farm, kasba, local bus, temple fair, small shop).

record.subtype: Smiling while crying, tears of joy [Interpreting]
record.passage:
The band had gone quiet and the jeep was packed with the bride's suitcases when Vaibhav noticed Yamini by the mango tree, wiping her cheeks with her dupatta and grinning at the same time. She had been fussing over her little sister's veil all morning. He nearly rushed over to ask who had upset her, then saw the grin was real. He walked up and said, "Can I stand here with you?" She nodded.
"She looked so happy," Yamini said, laughing and sniffing together. "And the house will be so quiet now. And I'm glad it's done, I was tired of worrying about the caterers."
Vaibhav passed her his handkerchief. "I'm feeling it too, honestly. Come, let's wave until the jeep turns the corner."
They did, both a bit wet-eyed.

qa.q: Where was Yamini standing when Vaibhav noticed her?
qa.a: Yamini was standing by the mango tree.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Yamini describe?
qa.a: Happiness that her sister looked so happy, sadness that the house will be quiet, and relief that the wedding worry is over. Her tears and grin at once fit that mix, though Vaibhav could only know by asking.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do that helped in the moment?
qa.a: He asked to stand beside her, listened, offered his handkerchief and shared that he felt it too. He did not assume she was upset.

qa.q: What might have happened if Vaibhav had rushed in asking who upset her?
qa.a: Yamini might have felt misunderstood and had to explain herself, and the shared moment could have turned into defending her happiness.

record.grounding: Illustrates crying and smiling at once at a wedding, joy, relief and loss together, with a listener who simply asks and shares the moment.

row_description: A young child asks why endlessly about rain, bodies and rules. Questions show thinking, and honest simple answers or a shared search build trust.
recipe_text: Scene set inside an institution: school, hostel, clinic waiting room, workplace, sports club, community centre.

record.passage:
At circle time in the school's nursery section, Minakshi raised her hand before Bhavna Ma'am had finished the rule. “Walk, don't run in the corridor.”
“Why?”
“So nobody falls.”
“Why would they fall?”
“Floors can be slippery.”
“Why is the floor slippery?”
Another child sighed. Bhavna Ma'am smiled. “You ask a lot of whys, Minakshi. At lunch let's go and look at the floor together, and you tell me what you find.” Minakshi nodded, eyes on the corridor door.

qa.q: What rule did Bhavna Ma'am give at circle time?
qa.a: She said, “Walk, don't run in the corridor.”

qa.q: What might Minakshi be wanting when she keeps asking why?
qa.a: She wants to understand the reason behind the rule, and her eyes on the corridor door show she is already thinking about the floor. Another reading is that she enjoys getting the teacher's attention.

qa.q: How could Bhavna Ma'am handle many whys in a busy class?
qa.a: By promising a shared look at the floor at lunch, as she did, she gives Minakshi a real path to an answer without stalling the whole circle.

qa.q: How might another child feel about the whys?
qa.a: One child sighed, so some may feel impatient waiting for circle time to move on, while others may be curious too.

record.grounding: A young child's endless why about a rule shows thinking; a shared search follows.

row_description: A toddler pats a crying friend or brings a toy to comfort, showing early care. It is an emerging sign of empathy that adults reinforce with warm notice.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in an urban Indian setting (city flat, colony, market, school, office).

record.passage: At the Delhi playgroup Uday fell off the little slide and howled. Harsha, also two, stopped mid-scoop in the sand and toddled over. She patted his back, said "Uh-oh, Ud," and went to fetch her toy rabbit and placed it in his lap. Uday hiccuped, hugging the rabbit. The teacher knelt. "Harsha, you saw Uday was sad, and you brought him your rabbit."

qa.q: What did Harsha give to Uday?
qa.a: She gave him her toy rabbit.

qa.q: What does Harsha's leaving her digging to go to Uday suggest she felt, and what else could it be?
qa.a: It suggests concern for him, since she patted him and brought comfort. She might also have been drawn by the noise or by his attention.

qa.q: Why did the teacher's words matter?
qa.a: By noticing warmly what Harsha did, she helps Harsha connect her own action with caring.

qa.q: How might Uday feel once he holds the rabbit?
qa.a: He may feel soothed and less alone, since someone noticed his distress. 🤍

record.grounding: A toddler pats a crying friend and brings a toy to comfort, an emerging sign of empathy that adults reinforce.

row_description: A young adult separates honest persuasion, which respects the right to say no, from coercion, threats or manipulation that remove choice. Pressure, isolation or secrecy are warning signs to discuss with trusted people.
recipe_text: An elder (grandparent, uncle, senior colleague) tells the story to a younger person as a memory or example, in their voice.

record.passage: Pranav, you asked why I'm careful about the "career club" your cousin talks about. I'm Ishita. At twenty-three a senior from my office, kind at first, invited me to weekend meetings. To begin with he persuaded me fairly: he said what it offered and added, "It's up to you." Later the tone changed. He said, "If you don't come, you're letting us down," asked me not to tell my parents about the meetings, and called my old friends "holding you back." I noticed I was scared to say no. That evening I told my mother, and later a counsellor at work, and I stopped going. An offer you can refuse is one thing. Pressure, secrecy and being cut off from people who love you is another.

qa.q: What did the senior ask Ishita not to do about the meetings?
qa.a: He asked her not to tell her parents.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when she noticed the change in tone?
qa.a: She was scared to say no, which warned her that something was wrong.

qa.q: What could Pranav do if he sees these signs in an offer?
qa.a: He can talk to a trusted person, such as family or a counsellor, keep in touch with friends, and say no without explaining.

qa.q: How might the senior's first friendly invitation have looked to Ishita then?
qa.a: It looked like honest persuasion, since he said "It's up to you," which is why the later change was harder to spot. 🤍

record.grounding: A young adult tells how honest persuasion that respects a no differed from later pressure, secrecy and isolation that removed her choice.

row_description: A young child judges sincerity by tone, eye contact and whether the other child stops the behaviour. Children this age may accept any "sorry" at face value and need adults to help check whether repair happened.
recipe_text: Before / during / after across a few days or weeks, in three short beats showing change over time; each beat happens on a different day.

record.subtype: Reading whether an apology is meant [Interpreting]
record.passage: On Monday Omkar, five, knocked over Hemant's block tower and said "Sorry" quickly, looking at the ceiling. Hemant said "Okay" but kept frowning. On Wednesday Omkar did it again, said "Sorry!" and ran off. Hemant's shoulders dropped. The teacher asked, "Did the sorry fix it?" Hemant shook his head. On Friday Omkar sat down beside him, helped rebuild the tower and said, "Sorry I knocked it. I'll be careful," looking at him. Hemant smiled.

qa.q: What did Omkar do on Friday?
qa.a: He sat beside Hemant, helped rebuild the tower and said sorry while looking at him.

qa.q: Did Hemant believe Omkar's Wednesday apology was meant, and what shows it?
qa.a: As not meant, since his shoulders dropped after a quick sorry and Omkar ran off. He might also simply have been disappointed about the tower.

qa.q: How can a teacher help children check whether repair happened?
qa.a: Ask "Did the sorry fix it?" and help them see whether the behaviour stops and something is put right.

qa.q: How might Omkar have experienced saying sorry on Monday?
qa.a: Probably as a quick way to end an awkward moment, without yet knowing how Hemant felt. 🙂

record.grounding: Shows a child judging apologies by tone, eye contact and whether the behaviour stops, with a teacher helping check repair.

row_description: A preschooler tells jokes that miss the punchline, uses nonsense words and giggles at silly rhymes. The child enjoys the pattern of humour before fully grasping why something is funny.
recipe_text: A note written by an adult who watched: caregiver, teacher, counsellor, coach or supervisor (their observations, plus what they did next).

record.passage: Note from Eshaan, nursery teacher. At circle time Mridul (5) told a joke. "Why did the chicken sit on the clock? Because... it was hungry!" He laughed loudly and the others laughed with him, though I doubt anyone knew why. Later he chanted "wibble-wobble-woo" to the rain rhyme. I said it back and he clapped. Tomorrow: a nonsense-rhyme corner. 🙂

qa.q: What did Mridul say the chicken was?
qa.a: Hungry.

qa.q: What might Mridul be feeling as he tells the joke?
qa.a: Playful and pleased at making others laugh. He may not yet grasp why jokes are funny.

qa.q: What did Eshaan do in response?
qa.a: He laughed and played along with the nonsense words, then planned a nonsense-rhyme corner.

qa.q: How might the other children see Mridul's joke?
qa.a: They laughed along because laughter is catching, not necessarily because they understood it.

record.grounding: Shows a preschooler telling a joke that misses the point and chanting nonsense words for the fun of the pattern.

row_description: A young adult with a difficult roommate or group project feels irritation building. Naming the issue early, using calm words and taking breaks prevents small annoyances from becoming conflict.
recipe_text: A note written by an adult who watched: caregiver, teacher, counsellor, coach or supervisor (their observations, plus what they did next).

record.subtype: Angry and irritated in shared living and study [Regulating]
record.passage: Hostel warden's note. Over the past two weeks Gargi has come to my office three times about her roommate Neelam's music, late lights and unwashed cups. On each visit she said less and her voice got tighter. This week she told me she was starting to snap at Neelam in front of others. I asked what she wanted to be different, and she said she just wanted quiet after ten. I suggested she tell Neelam calmly and early, when she's not annoyed, and take a short walk if she feels angry. She agreed to try that evening. Two days later, she mentioned it went better than she expected. Neelam turned her music down and apologised. I will check in next week.

qa.q: How many times had Gargi come to the warden's office?
qa.a: She had come three times in two weeks.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling as her visits went on, and what did she want?
qa.a: She was growing irritated, with a tighter voice each time, and she wanted quiet after ten.

qa.q: What worked for Gargi in handling the conflict?
qa.a: She told Neelam calmly and early and took a walk when angry, and Neelam responded by turning her music down.

qa.q: How might Neelam have felt when Gargi spoke to her calmly?
qa.a: Neelam may have been surprised and a bit embarrassed, since she apologised and turned her music down.

record.grounding: A warden's note shows Gargi naming an irritation early, staying calm and taking breaks with her roommate Neelam.

row_description: A young adult in a tense crowd notices rising chants or pushing, signals that a group may escalate. The wise response is to stay calm, keep an exit, avoid provoking others and step away if safety is at risk.
recipe_text: An elder (grandparent, uncle, senior colleague) tells the story to a younger person as a memory or example, in their voice.

record.passage: Hansa, you say you're going to the rally on Sunday and your mother is worried? Let me tell you what I saw at twenty-four. I'm Santosh. It was a festival procession, and the crowd was happy until two groups began shouting at each other. The chants got louder and faster, and people started pushing towards the front. My friend wanted to stay and film. My heart was thumping, but I kept my voice calm and said, "Let's go to the side lane now." We slipped out the way we had come in, walking, not running. A few minutes later a bottle was thrown. I never argued with the shouters or answered back. Know your exit before you need it.

qa.q: Where did Santosh suggest they go?
qa.a: To the side lane.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling while the chants got louder?
qa.a: His heart thumped, so he was alarmed, but he kept his voice calm.

qa.q: What could Hansa do before the rally?
qa.a: She can note the exits, stay near the edge, tell a family member where she will be and leave if pushing starts.

qa.q: How might Santosh's friend have felt about leaving?
qa.a: Disappointed at missing the filming, since the friend wanted to stay, though leaving kept them safe.

record.grounding: A young adult in a tense procession notices rising chants and pushing, keeps calm, avoids provoking anyone and leaves through an exit.

row_description: A young adult reads messages and emails and may misjudge tone, as brevity can seem cold or angry when it is rushed. Since cues are missing, checking with a call or a clarifying question is wise.
recipe_text: First-person reflective account by the protagonist, looking back a little (for 7-12 keep it simple and short).

record.subtype: Reading tone in text without voice [Interpreting]
record.passage: I'm Nazia, and I once spent an entire evening hurt by one word. My group-project partner Bidisha had messaged me, "Fine." That was all. I'd asked if she could send her slides by Thursday, and she wrote "Fine." No emoji, no exclamation, no "sure!" like she usually sent. I read it as anger. I stared at the screen for an hour, drafting a cold reply, then deleting it. Finally I called her instead. She picked up on the first ring, sounding out of breath. "Sorry, I was on the bus in the rain, I could only type one word! Slides tomorrow, promise." I sat there feeling silly and relieved. Now, when a message sounds cold, I try to ask before I decide it is.

qa.q: What single word did Bidisha send?
qa.a: She sent "Fine."

qa.q: What did Nazia feel when she read the word, and what was the actual reason for its brevity?
qa.a: Nazia felt hurt, reading it as anger, but Bidisha was simply on a rainy bus and could type only one word.

qa.q: What could Nazia do the next time a message seems cold?
qa.a: She could ask a quick clarifying question or call, instead of guessing the mood from a short text.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt when Nazia called?
qa.a: Bidisha was probably surprised and apologetic, as she was out of breath and hadn't realised how her one word sounded.

record.grounding: Nazia misreads a rushed, brief text as anger and checks by calling.

row_description: A young professional confirms decisions in writing with a line like just to confirm we agreed. It reduces mistakes, though repeating too often may signal distrust to a colleague.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in a rural or small-town Indian setting (village, farm, kasba, local bus, temple fair, small shop).

record.passage: In the small-town office of the water board, Imran wrote after every meeting: "Writing to make sure we are aligned: we agreed the pipe repair will start on Monday, and Parveen will bring the materials." Parveen, the field officer, had once given a different date by mistake, and the note saved them a week of confusion. But when Imran added the same line after a simple chat about tea timings, Parveen frowned. "Do you not trust me?" Imran flushed. "I am sorry, it is a habit." After that he wrote confirmations only when a decision or a date was involved, and he said it warmly. Parveen laughed and said, "Now it feels like help."

qa.q: What day did Imran's note say the pipe repair would start?
qa.a: The note said the repair would start on Monday.

qa.q: What did Parveen feel when Imran sent a confirmation after the tea-timing chat, and why?
qa.a: Parveen felt distrusted and frowned, because a confirmation for something so small suggested doubt. It could simply have been habit, which Imran said.

qa.q: What did Imran change that worked?
qa.a: Imran wrote confirmations only for decisions or dates and said them warmly.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt when Parveen asked if he was not trusted?
qa.a: Imran flushed and apologised, so probably felt embarrassed and worried he had hurt Parveen.

record.grounding: Rural narrative of a young professional confirming decisions in writing, which prevents mistakes but may signal distrust when repeated too often.

row_description: A young adult may take vows in marriage, religion, or a profession, which carry cultural meaning and legal weight. The seriousness differs by culture, so a person asks what the commitment means to each side.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative with a complication or constraint added (time pressure, little money, a noisy place, a missing person, bad weather), still faithful to the row.

record.passage: Rain hammered the registrar's office and the power cut out just as Disha was due to sign. Her grandmother's plane was delayed, so the seven-step ceremony would happen on Sunday, but the registry slot was today. Her partner Arun read the legal declaration by the light of a phone torch. Mehak, Disha's cousin and a witness, watched Disha's hands shake. Disha whispered, "For me today is the legal part. For you, is it the real vow, or is Sunday?" Arun said, "For my parents Sunday is the vow. For me, both." She breathed out, half laughed, and signed in the torchlight. Mehak couldn't tell whether the shaking was joy or nerves 🙂.

qa.q: Why was the ceremony split between today and Sunday?
qa.a: Her grandmother's plane was delayed, so the seven-step ceremony would happen on Sunday while the registry slot was today.

qa.q: What was Disha worried about when she whispered to Arun?
qa.a: She worried that the day meant different things to them, and wanted to know what today's signing meant to him compared with Sunday's ceremony. Her shaking hands might be joy or nerves, as Mehak could not tell.

qa.q: What would you advise a couple whose families value ceremonies differently?
qa.a: They can ask each other beforehand, as Disha did, what each ceremony means to each side, and not only in a whisper on the day.

qa.q: How might Arun's parents see today's signing?
qa.a: For them Sunday is the vow, so today's signing may feel more like paperwork than the real promise.

record.grounding: A vow can carry legal weight and cultural meaning that differ by side, so a young adult asks what the commitment means to each of them, even under pressure.

row_description: A young adult presses fingers spread on a table to steady nerves or uses a fidget object to stay calm, a healthy regulation tool that observers should not mistake for disinterest.
recipe_text: An interview-style or spoken monologue: the protagonist tells the story aloud to a friend, podcast host or interviewer.

record.passage: Okay, Urmila, Sumit here, you asked how I got through the placement interview, so here's the strange part. I sat down, the panel started introducing themselves, and my heart was going like a drum. So I pressed all ten fingers flat on the table and spread them wide, like I was holding the wood down. It felt solid. My breathing slowed a little. One interviewer glanced at my hands and I thought, great, now they think I'm bored. But when they asked about my project I answered properly, and the interviewer nodded. Afterwards I told them I'd been steadying myself, and they laughed and said they'd assumed I was just being careful with the table.

qa.q: What did Sumit press flat on the table during the interview?
qa.a: Sumit pressed all ten fingers flat on the table and spread them wide.

qa.q: Why did Sumit spread and press the fingers on the table?
qa.a: Sumit was steadying nerves: the heart was going like a drum, and the breathing slowed once the fingers held the wood down. To an onlooker it could have looked like boredom, which Sumit briefly feared.

qa.q: What could an interviewer do if a candidate keeps pressing hands on the table?
qa.a: Judge by the answers rather than the hands, and perhaps offer a friendly opening question so the candidate can settle.

qa.q: How did the interviewer read the gesture in the end?
qa.a: The interviewer took it as carefulness with the table, not boredom, which shows one gesture can be read in more than one way.

record.grounding: A young adult presses spread fingers on a table to steady nerves and worries it looks like disinterest.
